prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms are trapped at a magic wavelength and interrogated without perturbing the clock transition, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B051 alone, with Katori and Ye. After round 1 I am more, not less, confident of the physics. The distinct step is the magic-wavelength lattice: many neutral atoms are held tightly, free of Doppler and recoil shifts, with the trap shift cancelled between the two clock states. That is what makes 10^-18 reachable in hours of averaging, and it is not a consequence of the comb or of single-ion control. The result has been reproduced and cross-compared by independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE), including over long links, and it is already used for tests of constants, relativistic geodesy and dark-matter searches. Six of eight members list it with the same two names, but I do not rest on that count. I rest on the fact that the doubts raised were about novelty, priority and timing, not about whether the measurements are right. I would write the citation around the lattice and magic-wavelength idea and not around an accuracy record or the redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: The honest weaknesses remain. The 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize cover the enabling lineage, so a reader may see the lattice clock as the next step in a recognised line. I cannot settle from memory the priority among Katori's 2001-2003 proposal, Lemonde and colleagues, and the first lattice clocks, and Ye's credit is the more delicate of the two names because part of it is for accuracy records, systematics and the many-body clock, and part for the comb. The SI second has not been redefined, and a two-person prize leaves out Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Derevianko, Takamoto and others. Finally, I am an atomic theorist and the strongest voices for this candidate are atomic physicists, so we may be too comfortable with it.

responses.point: Pearce prefers B051 together with B009 (Halzen alone), as a prize about instruments that let us measure the Universe and time with new precision, and says the pairing risks being thematic rather than scientific.
responses.response: I see the appeal of the theme, but I do not think the clock needs a second part, and I do not think a theme is a reason to add one. The strongest argument for B051 alone is that it is a complete discovery-and-invention story that two names cover. Adding B009 brings in a one-name credit for a very large collaboration that you yourself say you cannot resolve from the supplied credit. I cannot judge that credit and I would not vote for a part I cannot judge, so I decline the pairing. I do agree with you on the citation: the distinct step is the simultaneous interrogation of many atoms at the magic wavelength, and I have put that in my text.

responses.point: Danielsson pairs B009 with B051 and says the Katori and Ye priority split against Lemonde and others belongs in a request to outside experts.
responses.response: I agree that the priority split should be checked against the original 2001-2003 papers, and I would welcome an archival note before the ballot. My preference does not depend on it, though. Even if Lemonde and colleagues had early ideas, the first working lattice clock and the demonstration of the cancellation of the trap shift are experimental steps, and I am not persuaded that a third name is needed. On B009 I respect that it is a genuine new window, but a prize cannot be well founded on a credit that you say may need a second name. I would also not restrict the clock citation to an accuracy record, to avoid blurring it into the comb prize.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether Ye's credit is for the original invention or for later accuracy and many-body records, and whether a differently composed prize would be more defensible.
responses.response: This is the question I take most seriously. My answer is that Ye's group made the lattice clock a working system: it controlled the systematics and the density shifts, and in the Fermi-degenerate Sr clock the spin-exchange interactions had to be understood and then exploited. That is part of the clock achievement and not only a refinement, and Katori alone would leave out the step that made the idea an instrument at 10^-18. I accept that the citation should say 'invention and realization' and not 'accuracy', so Katori is credited for the idea and the first realisation and Ye for the realisation at the highest performance. If the archive showed that Ye's role was only incremental, I would reconsider and I would then support a one-person credit before a three-person one.

responses.point: Kroll asks that the citation name the invention and not an accuracy record, and invites challenge from condensed-matter colleagues on whether the impact beyond atomic physics is as broad as claimed.
responses.response: I agree on the wording. To your invitation, I should say that the reach beyond atomic physics is real but partly prospective: relativistic geodesy, searches for ultralight dark matter and tests of local position invariance are results of limits, not discoveries, so I would not claim more than that in the citation. I also do not want to carry the redefinition of the second into the text. I share your caution that we are two atomic physicists who may be too fond of this one, which is why I put B050 as my first alternative and not as an afterthought.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B050 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) alone and asks whether the missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang credit is serious enough to push B050 below the clocks for me.
responses.response: Thank you for the clear answer on 2016: Z2 topology protected by time-reversal symmetry is a different thing from the integer quantum Hall phases, and I accept that this objection is weaker than I first gave it. I still put B051 above B050 because of the credit. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the specific HgTe proposal that Molenkamp tested, so the theory-experiment story that is B050's strength is also the place where it is least complete, and the three-dimensional work is only partly covered. The clock credit has a smaller and more checkable gap. This is a difference in the credit and not in the science, and if an expert report resolved the BHZ question I would move B050 up.

responses.point: Johansson moved to B051 and asks whether Ye's many-body clock work adds to the concept in a way the citation should capture, or is only an engineering record.
responses.response: I lean the same way you do. The many-body clock is physics and not only engineering: in a dense degenerate lattice gas the interactions shift the line, and the clock had to be understood as a many-body system before it could reach 10^-18. I would capture this in the citation by the word 'realization' and by the phrase about many atoms trapped at a magic wavelength, and not by naming the many-body work separately, since that would invite the comb overlap and a longer list of names. This also means I did not change my configuration, but your point sharpened my wording.

uncertainties: The priority among Katori's 2001-2003 magic-wavelength proposal, Lemonde and colleagues, and the first lattice clocks has not been checked against the original papers; an archival or outside-expert note would help.
Whether Ye's credit is best worded as realization at the highest performance and the many-body clock, without blurring into the 2005 comb prize.
Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which is a judgement I cannot prove.
Whether the unfinished redefinition of the second should make recognition wait; I think not, but others may weigh it differently.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged. I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier and of Lund and ETH attosecond groups, which concerns attosecond physics and not lattice clocks, and I have no known tie to Katori or Ye. I work in atomic theory and may be sympathetic to atomic-physics candidates; Kroll has made the same point about himself, and I welcome challenge. I do not think this requires recusal on B051 or on the alternatives B050 and B027.
